pph.setting: Emergency admission; major bleeding may need theatre/critical care
outpatient: Active PPH, shock or suspected secondary PPH with systemic illness is not suitable for routine outpatient management.
admit: Admit and treat ongoing heavy bleeding, abnormal haemodynamics, suspected retained tissue/infection or coagulopathy. Transfer to theatre/critical care according to bleeding and organ-support requirements.
ready: The bleeding source is controlled; uterine/perineal/wound assessment is satisfactory and there is no recurrent concerning loss.

Haemodynamics, consciousness, urine output, oral intake, mobility and pain control support home care. Review anaemia symptoms, Hb trend and any coagulopathy/organ injury; there is no single Hb value that alone certifies safe discharge.
medicines: Prescribe iron replacement when iron deficiency/anaemia is present, using a documented formulation, dose and response plan; assess whether IV treatment or transfusion is needed before discharge.
Uterotonics and TXA used for the acute event are not automatically continued at home. Reassess VTE prophylaxis after bleeding risk has fallen.
tests: Record quantified loss, procedures, transfusion and latest relevant CBC/coagulation/renal results; assign a reviewer/date for outstanding investigations.
homeCare: Explain the cause and treatment, expected lochia, worsening-bleeding warnings, fatigue/feeding support and the future-birth haemorrhage plan. Offer a debrief and emotional support.

followUp.action: Book anaemia/Hb response review and communicate any organ-injury or transfusion follow-up to the responsible team.
Review bleeding, recovery, mental health and the future-pregnancy plan; review sooner for symptoms or major anaemia.

returnImmediately: Sudden/heavy or increasing bleeding, fainting, breathlessness, fever, offensive discharge or worsening abdominal pain require immediate assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Only for diagnosed postpartum iron-deficiency anaemia after bleeding is controlled.

aph-previa.setting: Bleeding requires hospital assessment; inpatient versus home surveillance is individualised
outpatient: An asymptomatic, stable low-lying placenta may be managed with a specialist outpatient plan; admission depends on bleeding history, gestation, access to emergency care and support.
admit: Any new bleeding, contractions or pain requires immediate maternity assessment. Admit ongoing/recurrent significant bleeding, maternal instability, fetal concerns or inability to reach emergency care safely.
ready: Bleeding has stopped, maternal observations and Hb assessment are satisfactory, and fetal assessment is reassuring.
A senior obstetrician has documented why home care is safe, transport/support arrangements and the planned birth setting/date.
medicines: Treat anaemia when indicated; do not discharge with an unspecified tocolytic or steroid continuation prescription. Reconcile any remaining scheduled treatment explicitly.
tests: Document placental location and dates of repeat imaging; assess blood group/antibody status and indicated anti-D after bleeding.
homeCare: Provide immediate-return instructions for any bleeding, pain, contractions or ruptured membranes and a route to a hospital with obstetric/transfusion capacity.

followUp.when: At the booked scan and obstetric review
followUp.action: Review placental position and update birth timing/place; review immediately if symptoms recur.
Confirm blood availability, transport and senior operative/anaesthetic arrangements.

returnImmediately: Any further bleeding, pain, contractions, faintness or reduced fetal movement: contact/attend the maternity unit immediately.

aph-abruption.setting: Emergency obstetric assessment; suspected acute abruption usually needs admission
outpatient: Abruption must not be dismissed because visible bleeding is small or absent. Home care is considered only after specialist reassessment of a resolved/uncertain presentation with a clear surveillance plan.
admit: Admit suspected abruption with pain, tenderness, bleeding, maternal instability, coagulopathy or fetal compromise; arrange timely delivery and resuscitation when indicated.
ready: Acute bleeding/pain and obstetric risk have been addressed; maternal blood/renal/coagulation trends and fetal or post-birth assessment support recovery.
No ongoing transfusion/organ-support need; the senior team has documented surveillance if the pregnancy continues.
medicines: Reconcile anaemia treatment and any indicated post-birth VTE prevention against current bleeding risk. Acute haemorrhage medicines are not routine take-home treatment.
tests: Communicate blood loss, Hb/platelets/coagulation/renal findings and the plan for abnormal results.
homeCare: Explain recurrence risks, future-pregnancy specialist review and urgent-return symptoms; support bereavement if relevant.

followUp.action: Agree obstetric/fetal monitoring if still pregnant, or early postnatal and anaemia reviews after birth.
Review hypertension, placental-risk factors, recovery and prevention planning.

returnImmediately: Recurrent bleeding, abdominal pain, reduced movements, collapse, dyspnoea or fever require immediate hospital care.

vasa-previa.setting: Specialist birth planning; emergency admission with labour, bleeding or membrane rupture
outpatient: If diagnosed antenatally without symptoms, hospitalisation versus outpatient monitoring requires an individual specialist plan; do not apply a universal admission week to every patient.
admit: Ruptured membranes, bleeding or labour with suspected/known vasa praevia requires immediate obstetric attendance and preparation for urgent caesarean/neonatal care.
ready: After antenatal assessment, a clear birth/emergency plan and reliable rapid access are in place.
After birth, use mode-of-birth recovery criteria and ensure any neonatal haemorrhage/resuscitation follow-up is handed over separately.
medicines: Document indicated antenatal treatment; avoid an unsourced routine home tocolytic course. After birth use the actual operation/postnatal prescription.
tests: Confirm the diagnosis and relevant imaging/birth plan with the specialist team.
homeCare: Explain exactly which symptoms require emergency attendance and which hospital can provide urgent caesarean and neonatal care.

followUp.action: Give the next specialist review and planned birth date/place.
Follow maternal surgical/postnatal and neonatal specialist plans.

returnImmediately: Bleeding, ruptured membranes, contractions or reduced fetal movements need immediate maternity contact.

pas-spectrum.setting: Planned specialist-centre admission; urgent admission for bleeding/labour
outpatient: Stable antenatal PAS may be followed by a specialist team until the planned admission; outpatient care needs a documented emergency-access plan.
admit: Bleeding, labour, membrane rupture, maternal deterioration or fetal concern requires hospital assessment. Planned birth should be in an appropriately resourced multidisciplinary centre.
ready: After surgery, no recurrent bleeding, sepsis or unresolved organ-support need; bowel, bladder, pain, mobility and nutrition are satisfactory.

Document any urinary tract injury, hysterectomy, retained placenta/conservative management, drains or planned further procedures. Conservative PAS management needs an explicit prolonged follow-up pathway.
medicines: Provide the actual anaemia, analgesia and VTE-prevention prescription with stop/review dates; antimicrobial treatment is indication-specific.
tests: Assign review of pathology, Hb/renal findings and outstanding imaging or specialist results.
homeCare: Teach wound/drain/catheter care when applicable; discuss fertility consequences, future-pregnancy planning and emotional recovery.

followUp.action: Name the lead obstetric/surgical team and dates for wound, blood, urinary and pathology reviews.
Provide a specialist monitoring schedule and rapid-return access; ordinary post-caesarean discharge advice alone is insufficient.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, fever, worsening pain, urinary problems, breathlessness or collapse require immediate assessment.

pul.setting: Early-pregnancy assessment; outpatient only with reliable ectopic surveillance
outpatient: Stable PUL can be monitored outside hospital when symptoms are mild, assessment is reassuring and the patient can return for blood tests/scans and emergencies.
admit: Admit/escalate instability, significant or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, collapse or an unsafe follow-up situation; assess urgently for ectopic rupture.
ready: Symptoms and observations support home care, but the pregnancy location/outcome remains unresolved. Do not describe an empty uterus or falling hCG as proof of no ectopic risk.
Give written instructions, a 24-hour contact route and a named owner for every pending hCG/scan.
medicines: Do not give methotrexate merely because the pregnancy location is unknown. Reconcile other pregnancy medicines and RhD assessment as indicated.
tests: NICE: obtain paired hCG as close as possible to 48 hours apart, not earlier; symptoms take priority over the numeric trend. Arrange repeat ultrasound or review from the actual hCG/clinical pathway.
homeCare: Explain the diagnostic uncertainty and that an ectopic pregnancy can still deteriorate during follow-up.

followUp.when: About 48 hours from the first hCG
followUp.action: Review the paired result and decide the next scan/test or urgent assessment.
Track completion of the agreed pathway; contact the patient about missed or abnormal results.

returnImmediately: New/worsening unilateral pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, fainting or heavy bleeding: attend emergency care immediately, regardless of prior hCG results.

ectopic-pregnancy.setting: Emergency admission if rupture/instability; selected stable cases can be managed as outpatients
outpatient: Expectant or methotrexate treatment requires documented eligibility, no significant pain/instability and reliable access to serial hCG and emergency care.
admit: Suspected rupture, instability, significant pain or major bleeding requires admission and urgent surgery. Inability to return for follow-up or surgical-treatment criteria changes the management choice.
ready: After surgery: observations, bleeding, pain, oral intake, mobilisation and voiding are satisfactory, with review of operative findings/complications.

After medical/expectant selection: treatment and follow-up eligibility are confirmed, hCG appointments are booked and emergency access is feasible. Discharge does not mean that rupture risk has ended.
medicines: If methotrexate was administered, give the checked regimen-specific interaction, breastfeeding and contraception advice. No automatic repeat dose is a discharge instruction.
After surgery provide the indicated oral analgesic and review any VTE/anti-D requirements.
tests: Methotrexate: hCG on days 4 and 7, then weekly until negative, with review of inadequate fall/plateau/rise.

Expectant management: hCG days 2, 4 and 7, then weekly if the expected fall occurs. After salpingotomy: hCG at day 7 then weekly; after salpingectomy: urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks, review if positive.
homeCare: Give written rupture symptoms, avoid becoming pregnant until the methotrexate follow-up/contraception interval is completed, and arrange an early assessment in the next pregnancy.

followUp.action: Book the exact hCG/urine-test schedule for the treatment received; identify the results reviewer.
Review recovery, fertility implications, contraception and early scanning in a future pregnancy.

returnImmediately: Increasing abdominal/shoulder-tip pain, faintness, collapse, heavy bleeding, breathlessness or fever requires immediate assessment.

medicineDetails.when: For uncomplicated postoperative pain when prescribed; increasing pain still needs assessment.

miscarriage-management.setting: Usually outpatient/day care if stable; admit haemorrhage, infection or unsafe symptoms
outpatient: Confirmed uncomplicated miscarriage can be managed expectantly, medically or by day-case surgery according to clinical suitability and patient preference.
admit: Admit heavy ongoing bleeding/instability, suspected sepsis, severe uncontrolled pain or inability to complete safe outpatient care. Exclude ectopic pregnancy when the location/outcome is uncertain.
ready: Bleeding/pain and observations support home care; the diagnosis, chosen approach and possibility of incomplete treatment have been explained.
After evacuation/anaesthesia, recovery and postoperative assessment are satisfactory, with transport/adult support when needed.
medicines: Use only the regimen for the diagnosed type of miscarriage; provide analgesia and antiemetic treatment when needed. Review RhD care using the current applicable pathway.
tests: NICE: after expectant management, review completion at 7–14 days; if symptoms resolve, provide a urine pregnancy test for 3 weeks.
After medical management, urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks; a positive result or persistent bleeding, pain or fever needs assessment even when a test is negative.
homeCare: Explain expected bleeding/tissue passage, pain relief, hygiene and how to contact the early-pregnancy service. Offer grief support and contraception/future pregnancy advice.

followUp.when: If bleeding has not begun within 48 hours of misoprostol
followUp.action: Contact the treating service for review rather than repeating treatment independently.
Check the home pregnancy test and symptoms; arrange review for a positive result or ongoing concerns.

returnImmediately: Very heavy bleeding, fainting, severe/worsening pain, fever or offensive discharge needs urgent care.

medicineDetails.when: Pain relief when suitable; provide the selected miscarriage regimen in the treatment section.

outpatient: A history of recurrent miscarriage without an acute complication does not itself require admission. Arrange supportive early-pregnancy and specialist assessment.
admit: Current heavy bleeding, instability, infection or severe pain follows the acute miscarriage/ectopic pathway; urgent mental-health assessment is needed for immediate safety concerns.
ready: Any current acute event has been assessed and safely managed; provide a named supportive-care route and an investigation/result plan.
medicines: Continue only treatment indicated for the current pregnancy/diagnosis; do not prescribe anticoagulation or progesterone for every history of miscarriage without eligibility.
tests: Assign review of indicated investigations and any pending histology/genetic results; avoid repeating a broad panel without a clinical reason.
homeCare: Discuss grief support, planning another pregnancy and how to access early scanning/support if pregnancy occurs.

followUp.action: Review results, possible causes and a written plan for the next pregnancy.

followUp.when: With a new positive pregnancy test
followUp.action: Contact the early-pregnancy/support service promptly for the agreed assessment plan.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, severe/unilateral pain, collapse, fever or inability to remain safe requires urgent help.

molar-pregnancy.setting: Planned admission/day surgery for evacuation; urgent admission with bleeding or complications
outpatient: After safe evacuation and recovery, most follow-up is through a specialist hCG surveillance service rather than continued hospital stay.
admit: Admit haemorrhage/instability, significant anaemia, severe pregnancy complications or a need for urgent evacuation; arrange experienced anaesthetic/transfusion support.
ready: Bleeding and physiological recovery are satisfactory; histology is sent and the patient is registered/referred to the trophoblastic follow-up service.
The patient understands that normal symptoms or one normal hCG do not by themselves complete surveillance.
medicines: Document indicated RhD prophylaxis, anaemia treatment and effective contraception. Chemotherapy is a specialist-centre prescription, not a generic discharge course.
tests: FIGO 2025: hCG every 1–2 weeks until normal; partial mole confirms normal again at 1 month; complete mole needs monthly hCG for 6 months after normalisation. Plateau/rise requires prompt specialist review.
homeCare: Give the histology-specific follow-up schedule, the results contact and advice to avoid pregnancy until the surveillance service clears it.

followUp.action: Name the hCG service, book the first sample and establish who communicates histology.
Review missing/abnormal hCG promptly; plan an early scan in a future pregnancy.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, fainting, worsening pain, breathlessness or severe headache needs urgent assessment; an abnormal hCG callback must not be ignored.

mtp-india.setting: Outpatient/day care or inpatient treatment according to gestation, method and clinical risk
outpatient: Use a legally authorised service and a method/setting appropriate to gestation, health, safeguarding needs and preference; uncomplicated early care may be outpatient.
admit: Admit haemorrhage, infection, severe uncontrolled pain, suspected ectopic pregnancy, major comorbidity or a procedure/gestation requiring hospital monitoring.
ready: Clinical recovery and bleeding/pain are satisfactory; treatment completion or the agreed way of confirming completion is documented.
Written information, emergency access and any planned follow-up/test are provided. Routine follow-up is not mandatory after uncomplicated care if adequate instructions and access are available (WHO).
medicines: Supply the method-specific medicines, pain relief and any indicated prophylaxis exactly as prescribed. Offer contraception if wanted; do not infer RhD or antibiotic requirements from an unrelated procedure.
tests: Record any pathology, testing or completion check that actually needs follow-up; make a clear plan for ongoing-pregnancy symptoms or uncertain completion.
homeCare: Explain expected bleeding/pain, how to access help, fertility return and contraceptive choices without making contraception a condition of discharge.

followUp.action: Agree whether follow-up is required, what test is used and who reviews it; provide emergency contacts.

followUp.when: If recovery is not as explained
followUp.action: Arrange review promptly; persistent pregnancy symptoms, little/no bleeding after medical treatment or an abnormal scheduled test requires contact.

returnImmediately: Heavy/prolonged bleeding, collapse, fever, offensive discharge or severe/persistent pain needs urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Analgesia when suitable; method-specific abortion regimens remain in Treatment.

labour-management.setting: Birth-facility care for established labour; postnatal discharge requires mother-and-baby assessment
outpatient: Latent labour may be managed at home only after assessment excludes complications and the woman has a safe return plan. TOLAC requires a facility with immediate access to caesarean/transfusion when labour is established.
admit: Established labour/birth, concerning maternal observations, abnormal fetal assessment, significant bleeding, rupture of membranes with risk factors, or a need for analgesia/monitoring requires the appropriate maternity setting.
Scar pain, collapse, bleeding or fetal bradycardia during TOLAC requires urgent assessment for rupture and operative care.
ready: After an uncomplicated vaginal birth, the Indian NHM pathway keeps the woman under observation for at least 48 hours. The international WHO minimum is 24 hours; local clinical needs may require longer.
Before home care assess bleeding/uterine tone, observations, pain/perineum, bladder function and mobility; assess the newborn separately and observe an effective feed or document a safe feeding plan.
medicines: Reconcile prescribed postnatal supplements, pain relief and any indicated VTE/anti-D care. Routine birth does not create a blanket need for take-home antibiotics.
For TOLAC ending in caesarean or a significant complication, use that recovery/discharge pathway instead of the uncomplicated vaginal-birth timetable.
tests: Review maternal risk/results and the need for Hb testing after significant blood loss. Record any maternal/newborn screening or result still outstanding and its reviewer.
homeCare: Discuss lochia, hygiene/perineal or wound care, bladder/bowel recovery, feeding support, contraception, pelvic-floor exercise and emotional wellbeing; give the maternity contact/transport plan.

followUp.when: Within 36 hours after transfer (NICE service model)
followUp.action: Arrange the first face-to-face postnatal contact; the local Indian service may organise this differently.

followUp.when: WHO routine contacts: 48–72 hours, day 7–14 and week 6 after birth
followUp.action: Ensure the actual appointment/home-visit arrangements are recorded; add earlier reviews for complications.

returnImmediately: Heavy/increasing bleeding, fainting, fever/offensive lochia, worsening pain, severe headache/visual symptoms, dyspnoea/chest pain or unilateral leg swelling need urgent care.
A baby with poor feeding, abnormal breathing, unusual sleepiness, temperature concerns or early/worsening jaundice needs prompt newborn assessment.

medicineDetails.when: For maternal pain when prescribed.
Postpartum only when bleeding, renal and other contraindications have been excluded.

vbac-tolac.setting: Birth-facility care for established labour; postnatal discharge requires mother-and-baby assessment
outpatient: Latent labour may be managed at home only after assessment excludes complications and the woman has a safe return plan. TOLAC requires a facility with immediate access to caesarean/transfusion when labour is established.
admit: Established labour/birth, concerning maternal observations, abnormal fetal assessment, significant bleeding, rupture of membranes with risk factors, or a need for analgesia/monitoring requires the appropriate maternity setting.
Scar pain, collapse, bleeding or fetal bradycardia during TOLAC requires urgent assessment for rupture and operative care.
ready: After an uncomplicated vaginal birth, the Indian NHM pathway keeps the woman under observation for at least 48 hours. The international WHO minimum is 24 hours; local clinical needs may require longer.
Before home care assess bleeding/uterine tone, observations, pain/perineum, bladder function and mobility; assess the newborn separately and observe an effective feed or document a safe feeding plan.
medicines: Reconcile prescribed postnatal supplements, pain relief and any indicated VTE/anti-D care. Routine birth does not create a blanket need for take-home antibiotics.
For TOLAC ending in caesarean or a significant complication, use that recovery/discharge pathway instead of the uncomplicated vaginal-birth timetable.
tests: Review maternal risk/results and the need for Hb testing after significant blood loss. Record any maternal/newborn screening or result still outstanding and its reviewer.
homeCare: Discuss lochia, hygiene/perineal or wound care, bladder/bowel recovery, feeding support, contraception, pelvic-floor exercise and emotional wellbeing; give the maternity contact/transport plan.
Document the birth outcome and operative findings, explain future birth implications and give access to a birth debrief.

followUp.when: Within 36 hours after transfer (NICE service model)
followUp.action: Arrange the first face-to-face postnatal contact; the local Indian service may organise this differently.

followUp.when: WHO routine contacts: 48–72 hours, day 7–14 and week 6 after birth
followUp.action: Ensure the actual appointment/home-visit arrangements are recorded; add earlier reviews for complications.

returnImmediately: Heavy/increasing bleeding, fainting, fever/offensive lochia, worsening pain, severe headache/visual symptoms, dyspnoea/chest pain or unilateral leg swelling need urgent care.
A baby with poor feeding, abnormal breathing, unusual sleepiness, temperature concerns or early/worsening jaundice needs prompt newborn assessment.

medicineDetails.when: For maternal pain when prescribed.
Postpartum only when bleeding, renal and other contraindications have been excluded.

iol.setting: Planned maternity admission or a specifically selected outpatient induction pathway
outpatient: NICE permits selected outpatient induction with vaginal dinoprostone or a mechanical method after full assessment, discussion and safety planning; this is not automatic permission for every drug or high-risk pregnancy.
admit: Maternal/fetal risk, abnormal assessment, labour, membrane rupture, bleeding, a concerning response to ripening or inability to return promptly requires inpatient care. Oxytocin infusion requires a monitored maternity setting.
ready: For outpatient ripening, maternal/fetal assessment is reassuring, the exact method and reassessment time are recorded, and contact/transport support is reliable.
After birth use the appropriate vaginal/caesarean and complication-specific criteria; completing cervical ripening is not the same as completing maternity care.
medicines: Document which induction agent/device was used and when; the patient must not independently repeat a dose at home.
Reconcile regular medicines and the planned next induction step.
tests: Record pre-induction fetal assessment and the scheduled repeat/return assessment.
homeCare: Give the planned return time and instructions for pain/contractions, bleeding, membrane rupture, side effects and reduced movements.

followUp.when: At the exact agreed induction reassessment time
followUp.action: Review cervix, maternal/fetal wellbeing and the next step; do not leave an open-ended return plan.
Follow the relevant postnatal schedule and any additional maternal/newborn review.

returnImmediately: Return with contractions, rupture of membranes, bleeding, reduced movements, severe pain or other concerning symptoms rather than waiting for the booked time.

outpatient: A caesarean operation requires a maternity surgical setting; antenatal planning may be outpatient until the admission date if no complication requires earlier care.
admit: Admit for the planned operation or for any urgent maternal/fetal indication. Haemorrhage, sepsis, instability or organ-support needs require increased monitoring/critical care.
ready: Afebrile and recovering well, with no unresolved operative/anaesthetic complication, concerning bleeding or respiratory issue; pain is controlled on an oral plan and oral intake/mobility are adequate.
The urinary catheter has been removed with satisfactory bladder assessment, or a named catheter/voiding-trial plan is provided. Wound, VTE risk and maternal/newborn discharge needs are reviewed.

NICE UK offers discharge after 24 hours only for selected uncomplicated recovery with home follow-up. This is not an automatic Indian postoperative discharge time; use local service policy and individual surgical readiness.
medicines: Use a defined oral analgesic plan: paracetamol plus ibuprofen if suitable, reducing/stopping as pain improves. Avoid codeine/co-codamol while breastfeeding.
Review the indication, dose and stop date for VTE prophylaxis; teach injections when prescribed. Antibiotic prophylaxis at surgery does not automatically justify a take-home antibiotic course.
tests: Arrange repeat CBC/other tests after major blood loss or abnormal findings and identify who acts on the result. Assign pathology review when tissue was sent.
homeCare: Explain wound hygiene, suture/clip removal if applicable, bladder/bowel care, progressive activity, feeding and contraception. Resume driving/heavy activity when recovered and able to perform safely, with local/insurance requirements met.
Offer a debrief after an emergency operation and record the uterine incision, complications and implications for future pregnancy.

followUp.action: Provide the wound/suture or catheter appointment if required, prescription stop dates and contact details.
Assess wound, bleeding, pain, mobility, feeding and emotional recovery; bring forward review for complications.

returnImmediately: Fever, wound redness/discharge/opening, worsening abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, urinary retention, dyspnoea/chest pain or leg swelling requires urgent review.
If a prescribed opioid causes maternal excessive sedation or the baby becomes drowsy, breathless or feeds poorly, seek urgent advice.

medicineDetails.when: Baseline oral pain relief when prescribed.
Combine only when the clinician has excluded contraindications.

shoulder-dystocia.setting: Emergency intrapartum care; post-event observation and newborn assessment
outpatient: An unresolved shoulder dystocia is not an outpatient problem. After resolution, mother and baby still need a post-event assessment.
admit: Manage in an emergency birth setting with obstetric/neonatal help; admit/continue care for maternal trauma/haemorrhage or neonatal injury/compromise.
ready: Maternal bleeding and perineal/anal-sphincter injury assessment are complete, with a bladder, pain and mobility plan.

The newborn has been examined for injury and neurological/respiratory compromise; any specialist assessment or follow-up is organised. Apply the postnatal observation pathway rather than discharging immediately because the shoulders delivered.
medicines: Provide the actual perineal-trauma/analgesia/anaemia prescription; antibiotics or bowel treatment depend on the diagnosed injury and repair.
tests: Document the manoeuvres, time course, maternal injury and neonatal assessment; assign pending investigations.
homeCare: Explain what happened, offer a debrief and support, and record the recurrence discussion/future-birth planning needs.

followUp.action: Confirm maternal injury/repair follow-up and the newborn team’s plan.
Review recovery, continence/pain concerns and a senior plan for future birth.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, fever, worsening perineal pain, inability to void, new bowel-control problems or newborn weakness/poor feeding needs prompt assessment.

outpatient: Cord prolapse requires emergency maternity care, not observation at home.
admit: Urgent birth and neonatal support are needed according to fetal viability/status and the obstetric situation.
ready: After birth apply the actual delivery/operation recovery criteria. Review bleeding, pain, urinary function and any anaesthetic complications.
The neonatal team has documented the baby’s condition, any resuscitation/injury concerns and follow-up.
medicines: Use the postnatal/operative prescription for the care actually delivered; the cord prolapse itself does not define a routine home drug course.
tests: Complete the birth/resuscitation record and assign outstanding maternal or neonatal results.
homeCare: Offer an explanation and debrief, psychological support and a written record of events.

followUp.action: Agree maternal wound/trauma review and neonatal follow-up if needed.
Review physical and emotional recovery and concerns about future pregnancy.

returnImmediately: Maternal heavy bleeding, fever, chest symptoms or severe pain and any newborn deterioration require urgent care.

breech-ecv.setting: Usually outpatient planning; ECV in a unit with emergency caesarean access
outpatient: Stable breech presentation can be managed through antenatal review and a documented ECV/birth plan.
admit: Bleeding, labour, membrane rupture, abnormal fetal assessment or maternal instability needs hospital evaluation/admission; ECV complications require immediate obstetric care.
ready: After ECV, maternal observations and the required fetal monitoring are reassuring; no persistent pain, bleeding or other complication is present.
Document whether ECV succeeded, RhD/anti-D assessment and the plan if labour starts before the next review.
medicines: Record any tocolytic given and indicated anti-D; do not provide a routine home tocolytic course after ECV.
tests: Record presentation and pre/post-procedure fetal assessment; organise confirmation/review if required.
homeCare: Give clear advice about fetal movements, pain, bleeding and membrane rupture, and the planned place/mode of birth.

followUp.action: Confirm presentation and finalise the birth plan after successful or unsuccessful ECV.
Contact the maternity unit promptly rather than waiting for the next appointment.

returnImmediately: Bleeding, persistent abdominal pain, reduced movements, contractions or rupture of membranes after ECV require immediate maternity contact.

ctg-fetal-monitoring.setting: Assessment/monitoring in the appropriate maternity setting
outpatient: A reassuring CTG supports, but does not alone establish, safe home care. Interpret it with gestation, symptoms, fetal movement, examination and other risks.
admit: An abnormal trace, persistent reduced movements, bleeding, hypertension, growth concern or suspected infection requires escalation and admission when further monitoring/treatment or birth is indicated.
ready: A competent clinician has reviewed the full assessment, resolved or explained the concern and documented any further test/birth plan.
Do not discharge a symptomatic patient solely because one CTG snapshot appears normal.
medicines: No home medicine is prescribed simply to improve a CTG. Reconcile treatment for the underlying condition.
tests: Record the trace interpretation, actions and any scan/laboratory result still needing review.
homeCare: Explain the finding and exactly when to return; continued/recurrent reduced movement is a fresh reason to contact the unit.

followUp.action: Book any indicated scan or repeat assessment with a named reviewer.
Repeat clinical assessment promptly; previous reassurance does not rule out a new problem.

returnImmediately: Reduced/absent fetal movements, bleeding, severe abdominal pain or fluid loss requires prompt maternity assessment.

ptl-threatened.setting: Urgent maternity assessment; selected low-likelihood cases may go home
outpatient: For symptomatic women ≥30 weeks, NICE cervical length >15 mm or, when ultrasound is unavailable/unacceptable, negative fetal fibronectin ≤50 ng/mL can support a discussion of home care after full assessment.
Do not apply these discharge test thresholds as a shortcut to every gestation or presentation.
admit: Admit diagnosed labour, maternal/fetal concerns, membrane rupture, bleeding/infection or an unsafe home situation. If assessment at ≥30 weeks cannot obtain the indicated tests, NICE advises treating as diagnosed preterm labour.
ready: No cervical progression or complication requiring treatment/monitoring; assessment suggests a low likelihood of imminent birth, and alternatives for symptoms have been considered.
Document the benefits/risks of home care, return instructions, gestation and neonatal/transfer considerations.
medicines: Document any completed/remaining antenatal steroid doses and their arrangements. Do not send an unspecified maintenance tocolytic prescription home.
tests: Record the actual cervical length or fetal fibronectin result and fetal assessment; a negative test does not remove every obstetric risk.
homeCare: Explain that persistent/recurrent contractions or other new symptoms require reassessment.

followUp.when: At the agreed antenatal review or remaining treatment appointment
followUp.action: Review recurrence and complete any scheduled care.

followUp.when: Immediately if symptoms persist or return
followUp.action: Contact/attend the maternity unit rather than relying on the previous negative test.

returnImmediately: Contractions, pelvic pressure, vaginal bleeding, fluid loss, fever or reduced movements require maternity contact.

outpatient: Established preterm labour is not a routine outpatient discharge diagnosis; transfer decisions depend on gestation, progression and neonatal capacity.
admit: Admit labour with cervical change or a high likelihood of imminent preterm birth; arrange appropriate steroids, neuroprotection, antibiotics/tocolysis when indicated and neonatal discussion.
ready: If labour settles, discharge is a senior obstetric decision after reassessing cervical/membrane status, maternal/fetal wellbeing and access to return care.
After preterm birth, assess maternal recovery separately and arrange the baby’s neonatal care; an ongoing neonatal admission needs a clear maternal support/accommodation plan.
medicines: Reconcile what antenatal treatment was completed and any remaining doses; do not continue magnesium infusion or acute tocolysis as home treatment.
tests: Communicate gestation, membranes, infection assessment and fetal/neonatal findings.
homeCare: Give a return/birth plan and discuss feeding, expressing milk and support if the baby needs neonatal admission.

followUp.action: Write the next review/treatment appointment and the receiving unit if symptoms recur.
Follow maternal postnatal contacts and the neonatal team’s separate follow-up schedule.

returnImmediately: Recurrent contractions, fluid loss, bleeding, fever, worsening pain or reduced movements requires immediate reassessment.

pprom.setting: Initial hospital observation; selected stable patients may later receive home surveillance
outpatient: RCOG describes hospital observation for a few days after PPROM, followed by individual consideration of home care if mother and baby are well and early-birth risk/access arrangements allow it.
admit: Admit suspected infection, labour, bleeding, fetal compromise, maternal illness or inability to attend monitoring/return rapidly.
ready: No infection/labour/bleeding or maternal/fetal concern needing inpatient care; a senior team has agreed surveillance, transport and timing/place of birth.
Counselling includes that complications can arise after leaving and a previously reassuring review does not guarantee continued safety.
medicines: Complete only the remaining portion of the prescribed latency antibiotic course, with the original start/stop dates. Record completed/remaining steroid doses; do not restart a full course because of discharge.
tests: Document fetal surveillance, growth/other planned scans and clinical/laboratory infection assessment. No single normal inflammatory marker rules out infection.
homeCare: Give the unit contact, monitoring appointments and advice about temperature, colour/smell of fluid, pain, contractions and fetal movement.

followUp.when: At the exact scheduled maternity checks
followUp.action: Review maternal symptoms/observations and fetal wellbeing; reassess admission/birth if concerns emerge.

followUp.when: At the agreed gestation or earlier complication
followUp.action: Confirm the individual birth plan and neonatal arrangements.

returnImmediately: Fever/shivering, offensive or changing fluid, abdominal/back pain, contractions, bleeding or reduced movements: return immediately.

medicineDetails.when: Only the remaining prescribed latency course; confirm the course has not already finished.

prom-term.setting: Maternity assessment; selected expectant management may be at home with a time-limited plan
outpatient: After assessment, discuss induction now or expectant management for up to about 24 hours when appropriate; take infection risk, GBS history/status and maternal/fetal wellbeing into account.
admit: Admit labour or an indication for induction/monitoring, maternal/fetal concern, bleeding, abnormal fluid or suspected infection. GBS-related circumstances may favour immediate birth planning.
ready: Mother and fetal assessment are reassuring, no condition requires inpatient care and the planned induction/review time is booked.
After birth, review the newborn observation requirements after prolonged rupture; maternal discharge criteria do not substitute for newborn assessment.
medicines: No blanket home antibiotic course for every uncomplicated term PROM. Document indicated intrapartum antibiotics and the remaining treatment only if infection is actually diagnosed.
tests: Record the rupture time, GBS history/status and maternal/fetal assessments; communicate duration of rupture to the neonatal team.
homeCare: NICE: during expectant care check temperature every 4 hours while awake and report changes in discharge colour/smell or movements. Give a clear return plan.

followUp.when: About 24 hours from membrane rupture if labour has not started
followUp.action: Offer induction under the selected NICE pathway; record the actual appointment and whom to call sooner.
Complete the relevant maternal and newborn observations and follow-up.

returnImmediately: Fever, feeling unwell, offensive/discoloured fluid, bleeding, reduced movements or labour symptoms requires immediate maternity contact.

fgr.setting: Specialist surveillance; admit if maternal/fetal findings require closer care or birth
outpatient: Selected stable FGR/SGA can be followed with a written schedule of growth, Doppler and other fetal surveillance and a planned birth date.
admit: Abnormal/worsening fetal assessment, concerning Doppler findings, reduced movements, maternal hypertension or another complication may require admission and delivery planning.
ready: The specialist team has reviewed current growth/Doppler/fetal wellbeing and documented why the surveillance interval and location are safe.
The patient has reliable access to the next test and urgent assessment; do not discharge with only a generic repeat scan in a few weeks.
medicines: Record any antenatal steroid/neuroprotection course and remaining appointments; no unproven home drug is prescribed merely to increase fetal growth.
tests: Give exact scan/Doppler/CTG dates according to the diagnosed severity and gestation, plus the responsible reviewer.
homeCare: Explain reduced-movement reporting and the circumstances that would bring birth forward.

followUp.when: At the booked specialist surveillance contacts
followUp.action: Review fetal and maternal findings and update timing/place of birth.
Reassess rather than waiting for the next scan.

returnImmediately: Reduced/absent movements, bleeding, fluid loss, severe headache/visual symptoms or abdominal pain requires prompt maternity assessment.

multiples.setting: Specialist outpatient care when uncomplicated; admit for complications or planned birth
outpatient: An uncomplicated multiple pregnancy does not by itself require continuous hospital admission; chorionicity determines surveillance and birth planning.
admit: Admit preterm labour, bleeding, membrane rupture, maternal illness or fetal concern; suspected TTTS/TAPS or other monochorionic complications needs urgent fetal-medicine assessment.
ready: The reason for assessment is resolved or has an agreed specialist plan; chorionicity, current findings and the next surveillance date are explicit.
After birth, assess each baby separately and complete the actual maternal delivery/complication pathway.
medicines: Reconcile indicated supplements and other prescribed medicines; do not prescribe routine home tocolysis simply because the pregnancy is multiple.
tests: Record each fetus’s findings, chorionicity and scan plan; ensure the family knows which service reviews results.
homeCare: Discuss preterm-labour symptoms, fetal movement concerns, feeding/support and planned birth/neonatal capacity.

followUp.action: Continue the named specialist schedule; increase intensity for a diagnosed complication.
Confirm date/place, fetal presentations and neonatal/anaesthetic plans.

returnImmediately: Contractions, bleeding, fluid loss, reduced movements, severe headache or breathlessness requires maternity assessment.

reduced-fetal-movements.setting: Prompt maternity assessment; home only after a reassuring complete review
outpatient: After a reassuring assessment, many patients can go home, but persistent concern or risk factors may require ultrasound and further review.
admit: Abnormal fetal assessment, persistent/recurrent concern with other risk findings, maternal illness or a need for monitoring/birth requires escalation and possible admission.
ready: The clinician has reviewed movement history, examination and gestation-appropriate fetal assessment and addressed the patient’s ongoing concern.
If a scan is indicated, its timing and reviewer are booked; RCOG describes ultrasound normally within 24 hours of being requested.
medicines: There is no routine take-home medicine for a normal reduced-movement assessment. Treat an identified underlying condition separately.
tests: Record CTG/heartbeat assessment and whether growth/fluid ultrasound is indicated; communicate pending tests.
homeCare: Advise the patient to contact the maternity unit immediately for another episode, even after repeated normal assessments; do not recommend waiting until the next day.

followUp.when: Within the arranged ultrasound/review window if indicated
followUp.action: Review growth/fluid and decide the further plan.
Seek maternity assessment again regardless of how often it has happened.

returnImmediately: Reduced/absent movements, bleeding, pain or fluid loss requires immediate maternity contact.

gdm.setting: Usually outpatient; admit acute metabolic or obstetric complications
outpatient: Stable GDM is managed with education, glucose monitoring, nutrition and a reviewed medicine plan rather than automatic admission.
admit: Admit suspected DKA/ketosis with illness, severe/recurrent hypoglycaemia, dehydration, marked symptomatic hyperglycaemia or maternal/fetal compromise. Poor control may need supervised treatment adjustment.
ready: The acute problem has resolved; the patient can eat/drink, monitor glucose and use any prescribed medicine safely, with supplies and a named reviewer.
After delivery, confirm whether this was GDM or pre-existing diabetes; persistent hyperglycaemia needs assessment.
medicines: Before birth, continue only the individually prescribed metformin/insulin plan and provide hypoglycaemia instructions.
NICE: stop GDM glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth and reassess glucose before community transfer. Do not apply this stopping rule to type 1/type 2 diabetes.
tests: Arrange postpartum diabetes testing, using one named pathway: India programme 75 g OGTT at 6 weeks; NICE fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks, without routine postpartum OGTT. Use non-pregnant diagnostic interpretation.
homeCare: Provide glucose/insulin supplies when indicated, nutrition/activity advice, feeding support and future-pregnancy testing/contraception advice.

followUp.action: Joint diabetes–antenatal review and an individual plan.
Book the actual postpartum test and result review.

followUp.when: Annually after a negative postpartum test
followUp.action: Continue diabetes surveillance and seek preconception testing for a future pregnancy.

returnImmediately: Vomiting/illness with hyperglycaemia or ketones, severe hypoglycaemia, inability to keep fluids down or reduced fetal movements requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Antenatal use only if prescribed; GDM treatment is reassessed/stopped after birth under the documented plan.
Antenatal individual insulin prescription, not a universal starting dose.

pregestational-diabetes.setting: Outpatient coordinated care when stable; hospital admission for DKA or severe hypoglycaemia
outpatient: Stable type 1/type 2 diabetes needs joint obstetric/diabetes follow-up, not routine inpatient care.
admit: Suspected DKA in pregnancy requires urgent hospital/critical-care assessment even when glucose is not extremely high. Admit severe/recurrent hypoglycaemia, inability to maintain intake or maternal/fetal compromise.
ready: DKA resolution includes blood ketones <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH >7.3, clinical recovery and a safe insulin transition; normal glucose alone does not establish resolution.

Eating/drinking and glucose/electrolytes are stable; subcutaneous insulin has been given with the required overlap and specialist review. After hypoglycaemia, the cause/recurrence risk has been addressed.
medicines: Never stop all insulin in type 1 diabetes. After birth reduce insulin through an individual written plan with frequent glucose review; the GDM stopping rule does not apply.
Provide insulin, delivery devices, glucose/ketone strips and prescribed rescue treatment; teach the patient/family what to do when unwell.
tests: Review renal/electrolyte results after an acute event and record retinal/renal follow-up; glucose logs/CGM do not replace clinical review of recurrent lows.
homeCare: Give sick-day and hypoglycaemia instructions, out-of-hours contacts, feeding-related hypo precautions and the exact pre-birth/post-birth insulin plan.

followUp.action: Diabetes-team review, education and a booked early contact; document the precipitating cause and prevention plan.

followUp.when: Within the existing joint pregnancy follow-up schedule / immediately after birth
followUp.action: Review glucose and doses promptly after treatment or physiological changes; do not wait for a routine 6-week check to adjust insulin.

returnImmediately: Vomiting, ketones, dyspnoea, confusion, inability to maintain intake or severe/recurrent low glucose requires urgent hospital care.

medicineDetails.when: Rescue treatment when specifically prescribed with patient/family training.

thyroid-pregnancy.setting: Usually outpatient; thyroid storm or severe decompensation requires admission
outpatient: Stable treated hypo-/hyperthyroidism can be followed with scheduled TFTs and specialist obstetric/endocrine care.
admit: Admit suspected thyroid storm, significant arrhythmia/heart failure, severe systemic illness or inability to take essential treatment.
ready: The acute cardiac/systemic problem is controlled, oral treatment is established and liver/thyroid monitoring and specialist follow-up are organised.
If Graves disease/antithyroid treatment affects neonatal risk, the birth/neonatal team has the relevant history and antibody/treatment information.
medicines: Continue the agreed replacement/antithyroid medicine; do not stop it solely because delivery has occurred. Record any postpartum dose change and TFT date.
Explain urgent action for possible antithyroid drug toxicity, including fever/sore throat or jaundice, and avoid routine block-and-replace treatment.
tests: Assign TFT follow-up after a dose change and the postpartum review; assess additional tests according to the illness/drug used.
homeCare: Give written medicine instructions, toxicity warnings and a neonatal plan when relevant.

followUp.action: Adjust treatment from the measured results, not symptoms alone.
Follow the individual replacement/Graves plan and ensure neonatal assessment when indicated.

returnImmediately: Fever with marked tachycardia/confusion, breathlessness/chest pain, collapse, jaundice or possible drug-related agranulocytosis requires urgent assessment.

anaemia-iron-deficiency.setting: Usually outpatient replacement; admit instability, severe symptoms or major bleeding
outpatient: Stable confirmed deficiency can usually be treated with oral iron or a planned infusion service when appropriate. The Hb value must be interpreted with symptoms, gestation and cause.
admit: Admit active significant bleeding, cardiovascular compromise, syncope, severe symptoms or a need for urgent transfusion/close monitoring. Consider proximity to birth and access to definitive treatment.
ready: No ongoing bleeding or physiological instability; the anaemia cause, treatment route and response plan are documented.
After IV iron or transfusion, the required observation is complete and any reaction has been assessed. Do not discharge only because an infusion finished.
medicines: Use a specific elemental-iron/folate prescription for confirmed IDA; assess B12/folate or other causes when indicated. Avoid duplicate oral/IV/OTC iron.
Postpartum anaemia treatment differs from a preventive supplement; specify what continues and when it is reviewed.
tests: Record Hb/indices and relevant deficiency investigations; repeat Hb after about 2–4 weeks of oral treatment and investigate an inadequate response.
homeCare: Discuss administration, side effects, adherence, diet and how to access the next test or infusion.

followUp.action: Check Hb response, tolerance and adherence; reassess the diagnosis if response is inadequate.

followUp.when: Before birth / after major blood loss
followUp.action: Reassess urgency, replacement progress and any specialist/transfusion plan.

returnImmediately: New chest pain, breathlessness at rest, fainting, rapid deterioration or recurrent heavy bleeding requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: For confirmed antenatal iron-deficiency anaemia.
For diagnosed postpartum iron-deficiency anaemia after the acute cause is controlled.

vte.setting: Urgent hospital assessment; outpatient treatment only through a suitable specialist pathway
outpatient: Selected stable DVT/low-risk patients may be managed outside hospital only after specialist assessment, a safe anticoagulation plan and reliable follow-up/support.
admit: Suspected PE, haemodynamic or respiratory compromise, major bleeding risk, severe pain, extensive thrombosis or unsafe home treatment requires hospital care; unstable PE needs urgent critical-care treatment.
ready: The diagnosis/continuing investigation plan and anticoagulation indication are clear; oxygenation/haemodynamics and bleeding risk support the selected setting.
The patient can self-inject or has assistance, has medicine supply, understands missed-dose/bleeding instructions and has a birth/neuraxial plan if still pregnant.
medicines: Use therapeutic anticoagulation for diagnosed VTE, not the lower prophylaxis dose. RCOG treatment continues through pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postpartum and at least 3 months in total.
Reassess renal function, weight, bleeding risk and breastfeeding suitability; record exactly when to hold/restart around planned birth or procedures.
tests: Assign review of any pending imaging, CBC/renal findings and drug monitoring required for the individual patient.
homeCare: Teach injection technique, sharps disposal, bleeding precautions, medicine interactions and the contact route for planned labour/procedures.

followUp.action: Name the anticoagulation/obstetric reviewer, provide a supply and book the next clinical review.
Confirm the minimum course is complete and reassess continuing thrombosis risk; do not stop simply because leg symptoms improved.

returnImmediately: Breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, collapse, worsening unilateral leg symptoms or major bleeding requires immediate care.

medicineDetails.when: Only the selected therapeutic regimen, adjusted to the individual patient; not routine prophylaxis.

maternal-sepsis.setting: Emergency hospital admission; organ dysfunction may require critical care
outpatient: Suspected maternal sepsis with systemic illness is not a routine outpatient antibiotic prescription. A localised infection without sepsis may follow its own outpatient pathway after assessment.
admit: Admit suspected sepsis, hypotension, respiratory compromise, altered mental state, oliguria or inability to maintain intake. Arrange urgent source control and appropriate organ support.
ready: The source has been controlled or has a definitive plan; haemodynamics/respiratory function and organ trends support care outside hospital.

No unresolved vasopressor/acute organ-support need; an effective oral regimen or a formally supported outpatient IV service is arranged if antibiotics remain necessary. Persistent fever or deterioration needs reassessment.
medicines: Reconcile cultures with the actual infection diagnosis; give the selected antibiotic’s dose, route, remaining duration and stop/review date. Do not prescribe every sepsis example combination together.
tests: Assign a named reviewer and action plan for pending cultures, susceptibilities, pathology and abnormal renal/liver/blood results; ensure a patient callback route.
homeCare: Explain the source, treatment, risk of recurrence and post-sepsis physical/emotional effects. Provide written warning symptoms, 24-hour access and support for infant care if relevant.

followUp.action: Book the early clinical/antimicrobial review required by the source and organ injury, with the responsible team.
Review recovery, medicines, outstanding results and any specialist rehabilitation needs.

returnImmediately: Recurrent fever/rigors, confusion, faintness, breathlessness, reduced urine, worsening abdominal/wound pain or offensive lochia requires immediate reassessment.

hyperemesis-gravidarum.setting: Ambulatory rehydration or inpatient care according to severity
outpatient: Some patients improve after ambulatory IV rehydration and antiemetics and can go home with a functioning oral plan.
admit: Admit dehydration, inability to retain fluids/oral medicines, abnormal blood tests, significant ongoing weight/nutritional loss or comorbidity made unsafe by vomiting.
ready: Hydration and electrolyte problems are corrected or safely improving, oral fluids/medicines are tolerated and a nutrition/antiemetic plan is feasible.
Review weight, ongoing needs and the risk of thiamine deficiency; ketonuria alone is not a reliable severity or discharge measure.
medicines: Supply the selected oral antiemetic(s), with dose/frequency and how to reduce as symptoms improve; do not list all alternatives as simultaneous prescriptions.
Provide indicated oral thiamine; review whether iron worsens vomiting and assess VTE prevention for ongoing risk rather than automatically continuing inpatient prophylaxis.
tests: Record electrolyte/renal results and any repeat testing needed. Persistent severe symptoms later in pregnancy may require growth assessment.
homeCare: Discuss small tolerated intake, hydration, prescription supply before tablets run out and when to re-contact the maternity team.

followUp.when: At the booked early treatment review
followUp.action: Review intake, weight, medicines and any repeat electrolytes; bring forward review if oral treatment fails.

followUp.when: If severe symptoms persist beyond 20 weeks
followUp.action: Arrange maternity review and consider fetal-growth surveillance.

returnImmediately: Inability to keep fluids/medicines down, reduced urine, faintness, confusion, haematemesis or worsening illness requires reassessment.

medicineDetails.when: One selected formulation-specific option.
Only if selected after risk/benefit review; heed hepatic/QT cautions.
When prolonged poor intake makes supplementation indicated.

icp.setting: Usually outpatient specialist monitoring; admit concerning symptoms/tests or planned birth
outpatient: Stable ICP is commonly monitored outside hospital with symptom, bile-acid and liver-test review and a documented birth plan.
admit: Admit maternal/fetal compromise, severe alternative liver disease concerns, significant bleeding/coagulopathy or another obstetric indication; assess reduced movements immediately.
ready: The diagnosis and alternative causes have been assessed; results, repeat testing and timing/place of birth are documented.
After birth, explain expected resolution and the need to confirm it rather than assuming persistent itching or abnormal tests are normal.
medicines: Continue only symptom treatment that has been prescribed; UDCA does not replace the birth/surveillance plan. Routine vitamin K is not required for every patient.
tests: Arrange repeat bile acids/LFTs according to the clinical plan; at the 6-week postnatal check confirm symptoms and blood tests have resolved, with further assessment if not.
homeCare: Provide the fetal-movement and urgent-contact plan and explain how bile-acid results affect birth timing.

followUp.action: Review the current result and birth plan rather than relying on an old peak alone.
Check symptom resolution and liver/bile-acid results; refer persistent abnormalities.

returnImmediately: Reduced movements, jaundice, bleeding, severe upper abdominal pain, fever or systemic illness requires prompt assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Only when prescribed for maternal symptoms; review continuation after birth.

asthma-epilepsy-cardiac-ckd-autoimmune.setting: Stable disease: coordinated outpatient care; acute decompensation: hospital assessment
outpatient: A stable chronic diagnosis alone does not mandate admission. A named respiratory, neurological, cardiac, renal or rheumatology plan is required for the actual condition.
admit: Severe breathlessness/hypoxia, chest pain/syncope, prolonged/recurrent seizure, acute kidney injury/oliguria, severe hypertension or systemic autoimmune/obstetric deterioration requires urgent hospital assessment and appropriate admission.
ready: The acute problem is resolved and the relevant specialty has agreed treatment, monitoring and the safe care setting.
Persistent organ dysfunction, oxygen/infusion requirements or an unexplained seizure must not be covered by a generic discharge checklist.
medicines: Reconcile each disease-specific medicine, pregnancy/postpartum changes, renal dosing and breastfeeding safety. Do not abruptly stop essential anti-seizure, cardiac or steroid treatment without a specialist plan.
tests: Document the actual disease/organ results, pending investigations and named specialty reviewer; test schedules depend on that diagnosis.
homeCare: Give an illness-specific action plan, medication access and clear emergency contacts.

followUp.action: Book the actual specialty/maternity follow-up and tests for the diagnosed condition.

followUp.when: After birth or a major medicine change
followUp.action: Arrange early reassessment rather than assuming the prepregnancy regimen remains suitable.

returnImmediately: Breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, seizure, severe headache, reduced urine or rapid deterioration needs urgent hospital care.
asthma-epilepsy-cardiac-ckd-autoimmune.scopeNote: Triage and handover guidance for a multi-condition index. This is not a complete asthma, epilepsy, cardiac, renal or autoimmune discharge protocol; the relevant specialty plan must be attached.

uti-pyelonephritis.setting: Cystitis often outpatient; pregnancy pyelonephritis initially inpatient under the ACOG pathway
outpatient: Stable lower UTI without fever/flank pain or systemic illness can usually be treated orally with culture-guided follow-up.
admit: Suspected pyelonephritis in pregnancy: initial inpatient management (ACOG). Admit sepsis, dehydration, vomiting/inability to take treatment, obstruction concerns or maternal/fetal compromise.
ready: Clinical improvement, stable observations, adequate oral intake and a culture-directed treatment plan; investigate persistent fever/pain or failure to improve.
A suitable oral step-down or supported treatment service is arranged; nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin are not renal-tissue step-down treatment for pyelonephritis.
medicines: For pyelonephritis, the selected ACOG regimen completes 14 days total, counting inpatient and outpatient treatment; prescribe the remaining days and a culture-appropriate drug.
For lower UTI, use the separate complete pregnancy-compatible regimen and avoid restarting a full course at discharge.
tests: A named clinician reviews culture/susceptibility and contacts the patient if treatment changes. Record the chosen repeat-culture/recurrence plan.
homeCare: Explain hydration, treatment completion and the difference between bladder symptoms and signs of upper/systemic infection.

followUp.when: If not improving within 48 hours of treatment
followUp.action: Reassess promptly for resistance, obstruction or another diagnosis.
Confirm susceptibility and clinical response; arrange further testing/suppression only when indicated.

returnImmediately: Fever/rigors, flank pain, vomiting, reduced urine, faintness, worsening illness, contractions or reduced movements needs urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Lower-tract infection only when appropriate; not pyelonephritis step-down.
This displayed regimen is for lower UTI; do not use it as a universal upper-UTI prescription.

outpatient: Suspected intra-amniotic infection is not a home-observation diagnosis.
admit: Admit suspected infection and assess for maternal sepsis, fetal compromise and the need for birth/source control.
ready: After birth/source control, maternal condition and observations are improving with no unresolved sepsis or obstetric complication.
The neonatal team has received the infection, antibiotic and membrane-rupture history and made the baby’s separate observation/treatment plan.
medicines: Document the actual antimicrobial indication, culture results and whether further post-birth therapy is needed; prolonged home antibiotics are not automatic for every treated chorioamnionitis case.
tests: Assign culture/pathology review and repeat maternal organ/blood tests if abnormal.
homeCare: Give postpartum infection and bleeding warnings, feeding support and a contact route; explain any neonatal stay.

followUp.action: Name the reviewer of outstanding microbiology and any antibiotic stop/review decision.
Review fever, pain, lochia, wound status and maternal/newborn recovery.

returnImmediately: Fever/rigors, offensive lochia, worsening abdominal/wound pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or newborn illness requires urgent reassessment.

gbs.setting: Usually outpatient colonisation care; admission follows labour, membrane rupture or infection
outpatient: GBS colonisation alone does not require hospital admission or routine antenatal eradication antibiotics. A symptomatic urinary infection follows the UTI pathway.
admit: Labour/membrane rupture needs the documented maternity/antibiotic plan. Fever, maternal illness or fetal/newborn concerns requires hospital assessment.
ready: Maternal postnatal assessment is satisfactory; the baby has a documented infection-risk assessment and any required observation/treatment.
Communicate maternal GBS status, intrapartum antibiotic timing and membrane-rupture duration to the newborn team.
medicines: Intrapartum prophylaxis is not a routine take-home antibiotic course. Treat a diagnosed urinary or other infection with its own complete prescription.
tests: Make maternal microbiology/urine results available to the maternity and neonatal team.
homeCare: Explain the labour contact plan antenatally and signs of newborn infection after birth.

followUp.action: Contact the maternity unit promptly to implement the recorded plan.
Follow the newborn observation/discharge and routine postnatal contact arrangements.

returnImmediately: Maternal fever or a baby with poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, abnormal breathing or temperature concerns needs urgent assessment.

sti-syphilis.setting: Usually outpatient stage-specific treatment; admit severe neurological/systemic disease or obstetric complications
outpatient: Uncomplicated syphilis can be treated through a specialist antenatal/STI service with reliable attendance for all required doses.
admit: Neurological/ocular/otic disease, severe systemic illness or a maternal/fetal complication needs urgent specialist assessment and possible admission/IV treatment.
ready: Treatment appropriate to stage/pregnancy is given or fully arranged, allergy/penicillin needs are addressed and the follow-up/partner plan is documented.
The neonatal team has maternal stage, serology, treatment dates/completeness and the infant assessment plan.
medicines: Use only the correct penicillin formulation and stage-specific course. Missed weekly doses in pregnancy can require restarting the course; do not simply omit a missed dose.
tests: Document baseline and follow-up nontreponemal titres with the specialist service; track treatment and repeat-testing dates and infant results.
homeCare: Explain treatment attendance, partner evaluation/treatment, reinfection prevention and symptoms after treatment that need review.

followUp.when: At every required treatment dose and serology appointment
followUp.action: Confirm completion and assess reinfection/treatment response.
Ensure maternal records and the infant’s investigation/treatment follow-up are available to the neonatal team.

returnImmediately: Neurological/visual symptoms, severe illness, contractions/reduced movements after treatment or an unwell newborn requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Only for the documented early-stage indication.
Alternative stage-specific course; not given in addition to the early-stage course.

outpatient: Uncomplicated chlamydia in a stable pregnant patient can usually be treated outside hospital with partner care and follow-up.
admit: Pelvic/systemic illness, significant pain, fever or a suspected obstetric complication requires assessment for PID, ectopic pregnancy or another cause and admission when indicated.
ready: Treatment is provided, tolerated or reliably arranged; partner management and pregnancy-specific follow-up are explained.
medicines: Use the checked pregnancy regimen and counsel about adherence and sex/partner treatment to prevent reinfection.
tests: Pregnancy: test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment and repeat testing at 3 months; further pregnancy retesting follows risk/programme guidance.
homeCare: Explain partner notification and avoidance of sex until the required interval/treatment completion and partner treatment are satisfied.

followUp.action: Pregnancy test of cure; evaluate persistent symptoms sooner.
Retest for reinfection and reassess ongoing risk.

returnImmediately: Fever, severe pelvic/abdominal pain, fainting or ongoing/worsening symptoms requires assessment.

medicineDetails.when: For the selected pregnancy-compatible chlamydia regimen.

sti-gonorrhoea.setting: Usually outpatient treatment; admit disseminated/systemic or pelvic complications
outpatient: Stable uncomplicated gonorrhoea is usually managed through outpatient STI/antenatal care with treatment and partner services.
admit: Disseminated illness, joint involvement, sepsis, severe pelvic pain or suspected PID requires hospital/specialist assessment.
ready: The correct site/weight-based treatment has been given or arranged and partner/retesting plans are documented.
medicines: Use the checked gonorrhoea regimen. Add pregnancy-appropriate chlamydia treatment only when indicated, not an automatic doxycycline pregnancy prescription.
tests: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea needs test of cure at 7–14 days; repeat testing at 3 months for reinfection. Persistent symptoms need earlier reassessment and resistance evaluation.
homeCare: Give partner-treatment and sex-avoidance instructions and explain why persistent symptoms must be reported.

followUp.action: Complete test of cure with the treating service.
Retest for reinfection; arrange earlier review for symptoms or a resistance concern.

returnImmediately: Fever, joint pain/swelling, severe pelvic pain or worsening systemic illness requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Document the completed injection and indication; do not repeat it routinely at home.

sti-hsv.setting: Usually outpatient if oral intake and urinary function are maintained
outpatient: Uncomplicated genital herpes can usually be managed with oral treatment and a documented pregnancy/birth plan.
admit: Severe/disseminated infection, neurological illness, hepatitis concern, urinary retention, inability to take oral therapy or obstetric/fetal concern requires hospital assessment.
ready: Pain, hydration and voiding are satisfactory; oral treatment is feasible and the maternity team knows the infection timing/history.
Review birth/neonatal management when infection is recent or lesions/symptoms are present near labour.
medicines: Use the complete initial-episode or indicated late-pregnancy suppression regimen; these are different courses.
tests: Assign any pending virology and specialist/neonatal assessment results.
homeCare: Explain lesion hygiene, transmission precautions, partner discussion and why labour symptoms must be reported promptly.

followUp.action: Review response and the late-pregnancy/birth plan.

followUp.when: At labour or a recurrent outbreak near birth
followUp.action: Contact the maternity unit to reassess delivery/neonatal precautions.

returnImmediately: Inability to void, severe illness, jaundice, severe headache/confusion or an unwell newborn requires urgent care.

medicineDetails.when: For the selected initial episode.
Only for the separate late-pregnancy suppression indication.

vaginitis.setting: Usually outpatient; systemic/pelvic symptoms require another diagnosis to be assessed
outpatient: Uncomplicated BV, candidiasis or trichomoniasis does not normally require admission. Identify the cause rather than treating every discharge with every drug.
admit: Fever, severe pelvic/abdominal pain, systemic illness, pregnancy fluid-loss concern or inability to tolerate treatment needs assessment for another/complicated condition.
ready: The diagnosis, pregnancy-appropriate treatment and return advice are clear; follow-up is arranged for persistent/recurrent or uncertain symptoms.
medicines: Use the regimen for the confirmed/likely organism. In pregnancy use the selected topical azole course for candidiasis; do not substitute routine oral fluconazole.
Partner treatment/retesting is relevant to trichomoniasis, not automatically to every cause of vaginitis.
tests: Assign microbiology/STI results and arrange review if tests or symptoms do not fit the presumed diagnosis.
homeCare: Discuss treatment completion, avoiding irritants and relevant partner/STI advice.

followUp.action: Reassess the diagnosis and treatment rather than repeatedly self-treating.
Retest sexually active women for reinfection under the CDC pathway.

returnImmediately: Fever, severe pain, fainting, bleeding or suspected membrane rupture requires prompt assessment.

pid.setting: Outpatient for selected mild/moderate disease; admission for defined high-risk features
outpatient: Selected mild/moderate PID can be treated outside hospital if oral treatment, adherence and follow-up are feasible.
admit: CDC admission criteria include pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness/vomiting or temperature >38.5°C, inability to tolerate/follow oral therapy, lack of response, or inability to exclude a surgical emergency.
ready: Pain, fever and pelvic findings are improving; oral intake/treatment is feasible and the remaining course is supplied.

After parenteral treatment, oral transition is usually after 24–48 hours of clinical improvement. A tubo-ovarian abscess requires more than 24 hours of inpatient observation and a source-control plan when indicated.
medicines: Complete 14 days total therapy in the selected regimen, counting inpatient doses. Doxycycline/metronidazole step-down requires the appropriate nonpregnant context; pregnancy needs specialist inpatient treatment.
tests: Review STI tests and any imaging/abscess findings; arrange partner testing/treatment and results callback.
homeCare: Avoid sex until treatment is completed, symptoms resolved and partners treated; discuss reinfection and fertility risks.

followUp.action: Confirm clinical improvement; no response needs reassessment/hospital treatment.
Retest for reinfection; follow the abscess/specialist review plan when relevant.

returnImmediately: Worsening pain, fever, vomiting, fainting or no improvement within 72 hours requires urgent reassessment.

medicineDetails.when: Nonpregnant PID oral component only when selected; pregnancy is an admission criterion.
Remaining anaerobic-cover component of the selected complete course.

viral-pregnancy-hbv-hcv-hiv-rubella-cmv-.setting: Most stable cases need specialist outpatient coordination; severe infection needs admission
outpatient: A positive viral screen or uncomplicated infection does not by itself mandate admission. The actual virus, gestation, maternal condition and fetal/newborn risk determine care.
admit: Respiratory compromise, severe dehydration, encephalopathy, acute liver failure concern, sepsis or obstetric/fetal deterioration requires urgent hospital assessment.
ready: Maternal illness is stable, required antiviral/other treatment is accessible and relevant infection-control and fetal/neonatal plans are documented.
Do not apply one discharge schedule or medicine list to all viruses in this index.
medicines: Reconcile the disease-specific antiviral/other treatment with the responsible specialist, including breastfeeding and interaction considerations. Prevention of maternal-to-child transmission needs its own documented birth/newborn plan.
tests: Assign virology/serology, liver or other organ results and any fetal testing to a named reviewer; provide the actual review date.
homeCare: Explain infection-specific contact precautions, warning symptoms and how to access maternity/infectious-disease advice.

followUp.action: Book the relevant specialist and maternity follow-up, and communicate the newborn plan.
Review results and modify the birth/prevention plan when indicated.

returnImmediately: Breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, jaundice, persistent vomiting, reduced movements or an unwell newborn requires urgent assessment.
