aub.setting: Usually outpatient if stable; admit acute heavy bleeding or severe symptomatic compromise
outpatient: Stable bleeding/fibroid symptoms can usually be investigated and treated through gynaecology follow-up. Exclude pregnancy where relevant and assess anaemia and cancer risk.
admit: Admit uncontrolled heavy bleeding, instability/syncope, severe symptomatic anaemia, suspected infection or a surgical emergency. Acute pain requires assessment for other causes rather than assuming fibroids.
ready: Bleeding is controlled to a safe level, observations and symptoms are satisfactory and the investigation/definitive treatment plan is documented.
If a procedure occurred, recovery, pain, bladder function and complications have been assessed; anaemia needs its own treatment/response plan.
medicines: Use the selected bleeding-control/contraceptive or iron regimen with duration and review dates, after contraindication assessment. Do not prescribe all listed alternatives together.
tests: Review CBC and any indicated imaging/endometrial sampling; assign responsibility for pathology and persistent/abnormal bleeding results.
homeCare: Explain expected bleeding, what counts as deterioration, treatment adherence, contraception/fertility goals and access to the next review.

followUp.action: Assess response and complete evaluation of persistent bleeding or a suspected structural/malignant cause.
Check Hb response and investigate inadequate improvement.

returnImmediately: Very heavy bleeding, fainting, chest pain/breathlessness, severe pain or fever requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Only the selected heavy-menstrual-bleeding course after contraindication review.
For suitable pain symptoms; severe/worsening pain still needs assessment.

fibroids.setting: Usually outpatient if stable; admit acute heavy bleeding or severe symptomatic compromise
outpatient: Stable bleeding/fibroid symptoms can usually be investigated and treated through gynaecology follow-up. Exclude pregnancy where relevant and assess anaemia and cancer risk.
admit: Admit uncontrolled heavy bleeding, instability/syncope, severe symptomatic anaemia, suspected infection or a surgical emergency. Acute pain requires assessment for other causes rather than assuming fibroids.
ready: Bleeding is controlled to a safe level, observations and symptoms are satisfactory and the investigation/definitive treatment plan is documented.
If a procedure occurred, recovery, pain, bladder function and complications have been assessed; anaemia needs its own treatment/response plan.
medicines: Use the selected bleeding-control/contraceptive or iron regimen with duration and review dates, after contraindication assessment. Do not prescribe all listed alternatives together.
tests: Review CBC and any indicated imaging/endometrial sampling; assign responsibility for pathology and persistent/abnormal bleeding results.
Record the fibroid location/size and the planned imaging or surgical review; hysterectomy/myomectomy recovery needs the actual procedure-specific plan.
homeCare: Explain expected bleeding, what counts as deterioration, treatment adherence, contraception/fertility goals and access to the next review.

followUp.action: Assess response and complete evaluation of persistent bleeding or a suspected structural/malignant cause.
Check Hb response and investigate inadequate improvement.

returnImmediately: Very heavy bleeding, fainting, chest pain/breathlessness, severe pain or fever requires urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Only the selected heavy-menstrual-bleeding course after contraindication review.
For suitable pain symptoms; severe/worsening pain still needs assessment.

pcos.setting: Usually outpatient; admission is for an acute complication, not PCOS itself
outpatient: PCOS assessment, cycle/endometrial protection, metabolic care and fertility treatment are normally outpatient services.
admit: Severe bleeding/instability, acute pelvic pain suggesting another diagnosis, or complications of fertility treatment requires urgent assessment; OHSS follows the fertility-complication pathway.
ready: Any acute presentation has been assessed, a specific symptom/goal-based treatment is agreed and follow-up is feasible.
medicines: State why each medicine is prescribed: cycle/endometrial protection, metabolic care or monitored ovulation induction are different indications. Do not start ovulation-induction medicines without the required monitoring/service plan.
tests: Document indicated metabolic/endocrine tests, bleeding/endometrial assessment and the person responsible for results.
homeCare: Discuss cycle tracking, when prolonged amenorrhoea/abnormal bleeding needs review, lifestyle support, pregnancy goals and contraception if pregnancy is not wanted.

followUp.action: Review cycles, medicine tolerance, cardiometabolic risk and endometrial protection.
Use the monitored-cycle appointments and emergency contact arrangements.

returnImmediately: Acute severe pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or breathlessness/abdominal swelling during fertility treatment requires urgent care.

endometriosis.setting: Usually outpatient treatment; planned surgery or an acute complication may need admission
outpatient: Stable pain/fertility symptoms can be assessed and managed through a planned gynaecology/endometriosis service.
admit: Uncontrolled acute pain, systemic illness, heavy bleeding, bowel/urinary obstruction concern or another surgical diagnosis requires hospital assessment.
ready: Pain is manageable on a feasible oral plan, no unresolved acute complication is present and the investigation/specialist review plan is agreed.
After surgery, document what was done, any bowel/bladder involvement and the relevant postoperative criteria.
medicines: Reconcile the chosen analgesic/hormonal treatment with fertility goals, pregnancy possibility and contraindications. Provide stop/review dates for short-term treatment.
tests: Assign imaging, histology and fertility-related results; persistent symptoms need reassessment even if initial testing is reassuring.
homeCare: Give a pain/flare plan, activity guidance after surgery and a route to specialist support.

followUp.action: Assess treatment response, adverse effects and fertility priorities.
Review histology and any bowel/urinary/wound recovery plan at the agreed appointments.

returnImmediately: Worsening severe pain, fever, vomiting, inability to pass urine, heavy bleeding or postoperative breathlessness needs urgent assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Selected short-term oral pain relief when appropriate.

adnexal-mass-torsion.setting: Suspected torsion: urgent admission/surgical assessment; stable cyst: specialist outpatient pathway
outpatient: A reassuring, stable cyst/mass can be managed through a documented imaging/specialist pathway when malignancy/complication risk allows.
admit: Sudden significant unilateral pain, vomiting, peritoneal signs, haemorrhage/instability or suspected torsion requires urgent hospital assessment. A normal Doppler signal alone does not establish that torsion is absent.
ready: After torsion/surgery, pain, observations, bleeding, oral intake, mobility and voiding are satisfactory, with operative findings and remaining concerns reviewed.
A nonoperative discharge needs an explanation of the mass/uncertainty and a dated repeat-imaging or specialist plan.
medicines: Provide the selected oral analgesic and any indicated prophylaxis with clear duration; do not mask worsening pain with an open-ended prescription.
tests: Assign cyst histology or repeat imaging and document the responsible reviewer; suspicious findings need a specialist oncology route.
homeCare: Explain recurrence/acute-pain symptoms, wound care after surgery and the fertility implications of the actual operation.

followUp.action: Book pathology/imaging review and give the acute-pain return route.
Assess recovery, pathology and whether further cyst surveillance/treatment is needed.

returnImmediately: New/severe unilateral pain, persistent vomiting, faintness, fever, wound problems or breathlessness requires urgent care.

medicineDetails.when: For uncomplicated recovery when prescribed; sudden or increasing pain needs reassessment.

urogynaecology-core.setting: Usually outpatient; admit acute retention, infection, organ compromise or postoperative complications
outpatient: Stable incontinence, overactive bladder or prolapse is usually assessed through outpatient pelvic-floor/urogynaecology care.
admit: Urinary retention, sepsis, severe pain, obstructed/compromised prolapse, renal concern or a significant postoperative complication requires urgent assessment and admission if ongoing care is needed.
ready: Bladder emptying and pain are satisfactory, or a safe catheter plan has been established with support and a named voiding-trial appointment.
After surgery, no unresolved bleeding/infection/organ injury concern; mobility, nutrition and required home support are adequate.
medicines: Reconcile bladder, bowel, analgesic and any antimicrobial medicines, reviewing side effects/retention risk rather than automatically continuing every preoperative drug.
tests: Record urine culture, residual-volume/renal or other relevant findings; assign pathology or repeat testing when indicated.
homeCare: If catheterised, teach drainage/bag care, blockage warnings and who removes/reviews it. Give the actual pelvic-floor, bowel and activity instructions for the operation or conservative treatment received.

followUp.when: At the booked catheter/voiding-trial appointment if needed
followUp.action: Assess emptying and decide further care.
Review symptoms, treatment response and postoperative healing if applicable.

followUp.when: After stress-incontinence surgery: within 6 months; after prolapse surgery: at 6 months (NICE)
followUp.action: Arrange the surgical review, including vaginal/mesh examination when applicable. Catheter, wound and symptomatic problems require earlier review.

returnImmediately: Inability to void or a blocked catheter, fever, worsening pain, heavy bleeding, dyspnoea or leg swelling requires prompt assessment.

outpatient: Menopause/perimenopause/POI assessment usually does not require hospital admission.
admit: Heavy bleeding/instability, severe acute pain, suspected VTE or another serious acute illness requires urgent assessment rather than attributing it to menopause.
ready: Any acute concern has been excluded/addressed; the treatment choice, bleeding advice and review plan are clear.
medicines: Reconcile the selected HRT formulation and whether endometrial protection is required; discuss risks, contraindications and review. Do not stop or duplicate hormones without a plan.
tests: Postmenopausal or otherwise concerning bleeding needs appropriate investigation/referral; assign outstanding tests and results.
homeCare: Discuss symptom management, bone/cardiovascular health, sexual/urogenital concerns and contraception when still relevant.

followUp.when: 3 months after starting treatment, then annually (NICE); sooner if needed
followUp.action: Assess symptom response, adverse effects and unscheduled bleeding; provide the actual booked date.

followUp.when: Earlier for concerning bleeding or symptoms
followUp.action: Investigate rather than waiting for a routine medicine review.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, chest pain, sudden breathlessness, unilateral leg swelling or neurological symptoms requires urgent care.

gyonc-endometrial.setting: Specialist oncology pathway; admit acute complications or planned treatment when required
outpatient: A stable suspected/diagnosed malignancy does not automatically require emergency admission. Arrange an urgent named gynaecological-oncology/MDT pathway and track tissue/imaging results.
admit: Major bleeding, bowel/urinary obstruction, uncontrolled pain, dehydration, VTE, sepsis or an unwell patient receiving anticancer therapy needs urgent hospital assessment.
Suspected neutropenic sepsis is an emergency; only a specialist risk-assessed pathway can support later outpatient care.
ready: The acute problem is controlled and the treating team has agreed treatment-specific discharge criteria; oral intake, pain, mobility and any wound/drain/stoma/catheter plan are feasible.
The patient has the cancer-team emergency contact and a named owner/date for pathology, staging and the next treatment decision.
medicines: Reconcile analgesia, anticoagulation, supportive and any antimicrobial treatment with the oncology team. Chemotherapy/hormonal anticancer prescriptions are specialist- and regimen-specific.
tests: List pathology, imaging, blood/organ-function results and outstanding investigations, with the MDT/clinician responsible for acting on them.
homeCare: Teach care of any wound/drain/stoma/catheter; discuss nutrition, function, fertility/sexual health and emotional/practical support according to the actual treatment.
If hysterectomy was performed, explain the operation/pathology plan and any consequences for fertility and ovarian function.

followUp.action: Provide the booked oncology/MDT-result review and procedure/device appointments.
Follow the regimen-specific blood tests and 24-hour unwell/fever contact instructions; do not wait for routine review when ill.

returnImmediately: Fever/rigors or feeling acutely unwell during anticancer treatment, heavy bleeding, inability to pass urine/stool with pain/vomiting, chest symptoms or collapse needs immediate assessment.

outpatient: HPV positivity, screening abnormalities and uncomplicated colposcopy/biopsy are normally managed without admission. Ensure abnormal results reach the colposcopy pathway.
admit: Uncontrolled bleeding, severe pain, infection concern, an anaesthetic complication or suspected invasive cancer with acute complications requires assessment/admission as indicated.
ready: After biopsy/treatment, bleeding and pain are controlled and the patient understands what was done, expected symptoms and who communicates results.
medicines: Provide only the indicated analgesia or other procedure-specific prescription; routine HPV positivity is not an indication for antibiotics.
tests: Record biopsy/histology and screening follow-up ownership; a missed result is not an acceptable discharge endpoint.
homeCare: Give the exact bleeding, vaginal-product/sex and activity advice for biopsy versus LLETZ or another treatment; instructions differ by procedure.

followUp.action: Review and communicate results, with a fallback contact if no result arrives.
Complete recommended surveillance or treatment; new symptoms need assessment sooner.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, offensive discharge, fever or severe/worsening pelvic pain needs prompt assessment.

medicineDetails.when: Short-term pain relief when appropriate after the procedure.

outpatient: Routine contraceptive initiation, emergency contraception or uncomplicated IUCD/IUS care does not normally need admission.
admit: Severe abdominal pain, suspected ectopic pregnancy/perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, infection/sepsis or a serious medicine complication requires urgent assessment.
ready: The chosen method is clinically suitable, any procedure recovery is satisfactory and the patient understands efficacy, expected effects, backup needs and when to seek help.
medicines: Provide the selected method’s complete directions and any indicated emergency contraception, without duplicating incompatible alternatives.
tests: Record pregnancy assessment, any STI tests and a follow-up pregnancy test when indicated; assign results review.
homeCare: Discuss expected bleeding/side effects, relevant device warnings, STI protection and how to obtain removal or a change of method.

followUp.when: At the method-specific review/test date when indicated
followUp.action: Confirm correct use, testing and concerns; do not require unnecessary routine admission.
Review pain, bleeding, pregnancy concern or intolerance rather than persisting with an unsafe method.

returnImmediately: Severe/unilateral abdominal pain, collapse, heavy bleeding, fever or chest/VTE symptoms requires urgent care.

infertility-female.setting: Usually outpatient evaluation; admit severe fertility-treatment complications
outpatient: Infertility assessment and most monitored treatment are outpatient services; arrange partner evaluation and the indicated diagnostic pathway.
admit: Severe OHSS, pain not controlled by oral treatment, persistent vomiting/dehydration, reduced urine, breathing/chest symptoms, thrombosis concern or inability to attend monitoring may require admission.
Acute pain/bleeding after treatment also requires assessment for ectopic pregnancy, torsion or procedural injury.
ready: Pain/intake, urine output, observations and relevant renal/haematological findings support home care; the fertility team has agreed monitoring and emergency access.
Do not discharge significant OHSS with a generic pain prescription but no fluid, urine, thrombosis and review plan.
medicines: Reconcile the exact fertility medicines and any VTE prevention with the treating unit; avoid NSAIDs in OHSS because of renal risk.
tests: Assign pregnancy testing, imaging and any OHSS blood/organ tests to the fertility service with exact review dates.
homeCare: Explain fluid intake according to thirst, symptoms/urine monitoring, activity and the treating unit’s contact arrangements; provide postoperative advice if a procedure occurred.

followUp.action: Reassess symptoms, urine/fluid balance and tests; confirm the next contact before leaving.
Follow the early-pregnancy location/viability pathway, especially with pain or bleeding.

returnImmediately: Worsening pain/distension, vomiting, reduced urine, chest pain, breathlessness, leg symptoms or fainting requires urgent hospital assessment.

anc-overview.setting: Routine outpatient antenatal care; admit complications rather than uncomplicated pregnancy
outpatient: Uncomplicated antenatal care is organised through the trimester/contact calendar, with additional reviews for risk.
admit: Bleeding, severe pain, reduced movements, membrane rupture/labour concerns, severe BP symptoms, sepsis, significant dehydration or other maternal/fetal deterioration requires prompt maternity assessment and admission when needed.
ready: Any presenting concern has been assessed; mother/fetal findings support home care and a specific result/referral/next-contact plan is documented.
medicines: Reconcile supplements and any risk-based preventive treatment; an antenatal checklist is not permission to prescribe every preventive medicine to everyone.
tests: Write due dates and reviewers for the trimester investigations and outstanding results; late booking needs a catch-up plan rather than waiting for the next routine contact.
homeCare: Give pregnancy danger signs, contact numbers, transport/place-of-birth planning and the actual appointment dates.

followUp.when: At the next booked antenatal contact/test
followUp.action: Follow the trimester calendar and each investigation’s own window.

followUp.when: Earlier for symptoms or an abnormal result
followUp.action: Arrange appropriate review/referral promptly rather than waiting for a routine visit.

returnImmediately: Bleeding, severe abdominal pain, reduced/absent movements, severe headache/visual symptoms, fever/systemic illness, breathlessness or fluid loss requires urgent assessment.

hysteroscopy-aftercare.setting: Usually outpatient/day care; admit a procedural complication
outpatient: Uncomplicated outpatient hysteroscopy may be followed by home recovery once symptoms and the clinical assessment are satisfactory.
admit: Suspected perforation/organ injury, uncontrolled bleeding, severe persistent pain, infection or an anaesthetic problem requires hospital assessment.
ready: Pain/bleeding and observations support home care; recovery from any anaesthesia/sedation is adequate and transport/support instructions are met.
The patient understands what was done and when/how biopsy results will be communicated.
medicines: Provide a defined oral pain-relief plan if needed; further treatment depends on the actual procedure/findings.
tests: Name the reviewer of histology and any other outstanding results.
homeCare: Explain expected cramps/bleeding, hygiene and the procedure-specific advice for sex/activity; give sedation/anaesthetic restrictions when applicable.

followUp.action: Communicate histology and further management; provide a contact if results do not arrive.

followUp.when: Sooner if recovery is not improving
followUp.action: Assess persistent pain/bleeding or infection concern.

returnImmediately: Heavy bleeding, fever/offensive discharge, severe/worsening pain, collapse or breathing difficulty needs urgent review.

medicineDetails.when: When appropriate for uncomplicated recovery.

critical-illness-aftercare.setting: Emergency admission; critical care and later ward/home transfer are separate steps
outpatient: An unresolved collapse, amniotic-fluid embolism or major organ dysfunction requires hospital care, not direct home discharge.
admit: Admit to the appropriate critical-care setting for respiratory/circulatory/neurological support and definitive investigation/treatment.
ready: The cause and ongoing risks have been assessed, acute organ support is no longer required at the proposed destination and the receiving team can provide the agreed care.
Before home discharge, organ recovery, function, oral treatment/nutrition, mobility and support are adequate, with rehabilitation/specialty follow-up for remaining impairment.
medicines: Reconcile all temporary critical-care medicines, continuing prescriptions and indication-specific anticoagulation; document what stopped and why.
tests: Provide a structured critical-care-to-ward handover and assign outstanding diagnostic/organ tests; ward step-down is not itself clearance for home.
homeCare: Explain the illness/course, likely recovery issues and physical/emotional support; address infant care, bereavement or safeguarding needs when relevant.

followUp.action: Name the receiving team, monitoring/rehabilitation plan and urgent escalation triggers.

followUp.when: At booked post-critical-care/specialty and postnatal reviews
followUp.action: Review organ/function recovery, medicines, mental health and outstanding results.

returnImmediately: Breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures, heavy bleeding or recurrent severe illness requires emergency care.

anaphylaxis-aftercare.setting: Emergency treatment and risk-stratified observation before any discharge
outpatient: Acute anaphylaxis needs emergency care. Home care is considered only after complete recovery and a senior assessment of recurrence risk.
admit: Admit/continue monitored care for persistent symptoms, repeated adrenaline needs, severe respiratory compromise, ongoing allergen absorption, comorbidity or poor emergency access.
Pregnancy needs obstetric/fetal assessment in addition to the general anaphylaxis observation decision.
ready: RCUK: selected fast-track discharge after 2 hours from symptom resolution requires prompt response to one early adrenaline dose, complete resolution, available auto-injectors with training and adequate supervision.

Observe at least 6 hours after resolution if two IM doses were needed or there was a previous biphasic reaction; at least 12 hours for severe reactions (>2 doses), severe asthma/respiratory compromise, continuing allergen absorption or difficult access/night-time safety concerns. Longer admission may be needed.
medicines: Prescribe/supply adrenaline auto-injectors when indicated, with device-specific training and two available devices under the RCUK/NICE pathway. Do not replace IM adrenaline with antihistamine-only advice.
tests: Record likely trigger, treatment/dose times, observation duration and any tryptase/allergy investigation plan.
homeCare: Give a written emergency action plan, trigger avoidance, biphasic-reaction warning and instructions to use the prescribed auto-injector and summon emergency help.

followUp.action: Confirm practical device access/training and a safe supervision/transport plan.

followUp.when: At the booked specialist allergy review
followUp.action: Investigate the trigger and confirm prevention/rescue plans; add obstetric follow-up when pregnant.

returnImmediately: Recurrent breathing/throat symptoms, collapse or rapidly returning systemic symptoms requires immediate rescue action and emergency help.
